lesson.title: Eight Crises: Erikson's Blueprint for a Lifetime of Growth
lesson.summary: Erik Erikson proposed that personality unfolds across the entire lifespan through eight sequential stages, each centered on a specific social and emotional tension that needs to be worked through.
lesson.body:
Sigmund Freud argued that personality was largely fixed by the end of childhood, shaped by how a small number of psychosexual stages were resolved. Erik Erikson, who trained in the psychoanalytic tradition but broke from Freud in important ways, argued instead that development continues across the whole lifespan and that what drives it is not sexual energy but social relationships, hence psychosocial rather than psychosexual. Erikson proposed eight stages, each centered on a particular crisis, a tension between two possible outcomes, that a person works through during a roughly defined period of life.

The eight stages, in order, are trust versus mistrust in infancy, when a baby learns whether the world is dependable, autonomy versus shame and doubt in toddlerhood, when a child asserts independence, initiative versus guilt in early childhood, when a child begins planning and initiating activities, industry versus inferiority in middle childhood, when a child compares their competence to peers, identity versus role confusion in adolescence, intimacy versus isolation in young adulthood, generativity versus stagnation in middle adulthood, and integrity versus despair in late adulthood, when a person looks back and evaluates the life they have lived.

Calling each stage a crisis does not mean something has gone wrong. Erikson meant it more like a turning point or a developmental task, a tension that everyone at that life stage has to work through in some way, with the outcome landing somewhere on a spectrum between the two named poles rather than at one extreme or the other. Resolving a stage well tends to provide a stronger foundation for the stages that follow, but Erikson did not treat this as a strict, unforgiving pipeline. Struggles from an earlier stage can resurface later, and growth in one area does not immunize a person from difficulty in another.

This framework ties together several themes already introduced. It is a stage theory, which means it makes a claim about developmental themes like whether change happens in qualitatively distinct steps or more gradually and continuously, and it leans firmly toward the nurture side of the nature nurture conversation by locating growth in a person's relationships and social context rather than in biological unfolding alone. The two chapters that follow zoom in on the adolescent stage, identity versus role confusion, and later chapters return to the adult stages when discussing the social clock.
